passages.happening:
In the first year of Darius, a Mede by descent, made ruler over the kingdom of the Chaldeans (verse 1), Daniel is reading Scripture. He understands ‘from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years’ (verse 2).

So he turns to God. He seeks him ‘by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Babylon has just fallen to the Medes and Persians, about 539 or 538 BC. Daniel, now an old man who was carried off as a youth, realizes that the seventy years Jeremiah foretold are nearly complete. The exile is ending. But he does not simply wait for it. He confesses the sin that caused it.

This is the one chapter in Daniel built around a written text. Daniel understands from the books. The first hearers were shown a prophet whose prayer begins with reading Scripture.

Jeremiah's seventy years could be counted in more than one way. Counted from Nebuchadnezzar's first move against Jerusalem in about 605 BC, when Daniel was taken, they reach close to Cyrus's decree in 539 or 538 BC. Counted from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC, they reach roughly to its rebuilding, finished in 516 or 515 BC. Later biblical writers were already reading the number as a word that could be reckoned more than one way.

Fasting, sackcloth and ashes were the ordinary signs of mourning and repentance in Israel. They were not ways of earning a hearing. They were ways of agreeing with God's verdict with the whole body.
passages.later: Jeremiah had written, ‘When Babylon’s seventy years are complete, I will attend to you and confirm My promise to restore you to this place’ (Jeremiah 29:10). And Ezra tells how the LORD moved Cyrus ‘to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah’ (Ezra 1:1).
passages.asks: Daniel read a promise that was nearly fulfilled, and it drove him to his knees rather than to waiting. Ask what promises of God you are reading, and what they move you to do. And ask whether your prayer begins with Scripture or only with your needs.

passages.t: A prayer of confession for a whole people
passages.happening:
Daniel prays to the LORD his God and confesses. He begins, ‘O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of loving devotion to those who love Him and keep His commandments’ (verse 4).

Then the confession: ‘we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled’ (verse 5). They did not listen to the prophets who spoke to their kings, leaders and fathers (verse 6). ‘To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but this day we are covered with shame’ (verse 7), the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem and all Israel near and far.

‘To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him’ (verse 9). The curse written in the Law of Moses has been poured out on them because they sinned (verse 11). God has carried out his words, bringing a disaster on Jerusalem like no other (verse 12), and still they have not turned from their iniquities (verse 13). ‘For the LORD our God is righteous in all He does; yet we have not obeyed His voice’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The prayer opens with words from Deuteronomy, used again in Nehemiah's prayer. It draws heavily on Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, which asked God to hear exiles who came to their senses in the land of their captors and said they had sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly. Daniel uses nearly those words.

The verbs pile up: sinned, done wrong, acted wickedly, rebelled, turned away. The refrain is contrast. To God belong righteousness, compassion and forgiveness. To the people, shame.

Notice that Daniel speaks in the first person plural. The book has shown him faithful all his life. Yet he confesses in the first person plural, because the covenant bound the generations together, and the Law itself named the sins of the fathers alongside the people's own. A leader confessing for his people does not stand outside their guilt.

This is the only chapter of Daniel that uses God's covenant name, the LORD, and it does so eight times. The prayer's Hebrew is smoother and more traditional than the rest of the book, which leads some scholars to think Daniel is using or adapting a known prayer of his people.
passages.later: Solomon had asked God to hear exiles who would say, ‘We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly’ (1 Kings 8:47). Nehemiah prays in the same way: ‘I confess the sins that we Israelites have committed against You. Both I and my father’s house have sinned’ (Nehemiah 1:6). And Ezra prays, ‘our iniquities are higher than our heads’ (Ezra 9:6).
passages.asks: Daniel, the most faithful man in the book, prays ‘we have sinned’ (verse 5). Ask whether you pray for your community as one of them, or as someone standing outside. And ask what it would look like to say that God is righteous in what has happened to you, without pretending it does not hurt.

passages.t: O Lord, listen. O Lord, forgive.
passages.happening:
Now the prayer turns to asking. Daniel recalls the God who brought his people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and made a name for himself (verse 15). He prays that God's anger would turn away from his city Jerusalem, his holy mountain, which has become a reproach to all around (verse 16).

‘For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary’ (verse 17). ‘Incline Your ear, O my God, and hear; open Your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears Your name’ (verse 18).

And he says why God should answer: ‘For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion’ (verse 18).

The prayer ends in a rush of short pleas: “O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
As the prayer rises, the possessive words shift from the people's to God's: your city, your holy mountain, your desolate sanctuary, the city that bears your name, your people. Daniel is reminding God that what lies in ruins is his own.

The ground of the request is God's character and God's name, not Israel's goodness. Daniel asks God to act for his own sake. The first hearers, who had nothing left to offer, were given a way to pray that depends on nothing they had.

The prayer has close relatives in the writings of that age. The book of Baruch, in the Greek Old Testament and the Apocrypha, follows Daniel's prayer phrase by phrase, and scholars debate which depends on which, or whether both draw on a shared prayer. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls are weekday prayers of communal confession of the same kind.
passages.later: Moses, too, pleaded with God on the ground of his name and his past mercy at the exodus (Exodus 32:11-12). And the priests were to pray over the people, ‘may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you’ (Numbers 6:25). A psalm prays, ‘Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved’ (Psalm 80:3).
passages.asks: Daniel did not plead his own goodness, only God's compassion. Ask what you are relying on when you pray. And ask whether you can pray for something because God's own name is bound up with it.

passages.happening:
‘While I was speaking, praying, confessing my sin and that of my people Israel’ (verse 20), Gabriel, the man Daniel had seen in the earlier vision, comes to him in swift flight ‘about the time of the evening sacrifice’ (verse 21).

He says, ‘O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding’ (verse 22). ‘At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are highly precious’ (verse 23). Daniel is to consider the message and understand the vision.
passages.hearers:
Daniel confesses ‘my sin and that of my people Israel’ (verse 20). He includes himself again.

Gabriel comes about the time of the evening sacrifice, though the temple had lain in ruins for nearly fifty years. The evening offering was made in the late afternoon. It had become a set hour of prayer: Ezra prayed at it, a psalm compares prayer to it, and later Jewish tradition traced the synagogue's daily prayers to the times of the temple offerings. The old rhythm of temple worship still shaped the prayer of the exiles, though there was no altar to offer on.

The answer went out at the beginning of Daniel's prayer. The first hearers were told something about God's way with prayer: he does not wait to be persuaded. And Daniel is told that he is highly precious, a word of tenderness from heaven to an old man in exile.
passages.later: A psalm prays, ‘May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering’ (Psalm 141:2). Isaiah hears the LORD promise, ‘Even before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will hear’ (Isaiah 65:24).
passages.asks: The answer went out at the beginning of Daniel's prayer, and he was told he was highly precious. Ask whether you believe God is that ready to hear you. And ask what it would change if you believed that you, too, are precious to him.

passages.happening:
Gabriel says, ‘Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place’ (verse 24).

From the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until an anointed one, a prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. The city will be rebuilt, ‘but in times of distress’ (verse 25).

After the sixty-two weeks the anointed one will be cut off and have nothing. The people of a prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. ‘The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed’ (verse 26).

And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week put an end to sacrifice and offering. ‘And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Gabriel's answer is compressed and allusive, built on a play with sevens. Jeremiah's seventy years become seventy weeks, usually understood as seventy sevens of years, divided into seven, sixty-two and one. Israel's calendar was built on sevens. Every seventh year was a sabbath for the land, and after seven sevens of years came the jubilee, when debts were released and land returned to its families. Seventy sevens is 490 years, ten jubilees, a small sabbath pattern magnified into a great release.

Verse 24 lists six purposes, often read as three pairs: three dealing with sin, and three with what God will bring. Then verses 25 to 27 walk through the periods, and the language turns dark: an anointed one cut off, a prince whose people destroy, a flood, war, desolations and an abomination.

The BSB writes the Messiah, the Prince, and the Messiah will be cut off. The Hebrew has no article. Mashiach means an anointed one, and who is meant is one of the chief questions in dispute.

The first hearers were told that the return from Babylon would not be the end of their troubles. The city would be rebuilt in times of distress, and more suffering would come before sin was finally dealt with. The chapter ends not with the six purposes fulfilled but with destruction poured out on the destroyer, leaving the reader, like Daniel, holding the promise and the pain together.
passages.later: Jesus spoke of ‘the abomination of desolation,’ described by the prophet Daniel (Matthew 24:15), as he foretold the destruction of the temple. The law of the jubilee had said, ‘proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants’ (Leviticus 25:10).
passages.hard:
What are the seventy weeks, and who is the anointed one who is cut off?

This is one of the most debated passages in the Bible, and every reading has real strengths and real difficulties. Jewish interpreters have argued that it concerns the Second Temple and its fall, not the Messiah. One old Jewish chronology counts seventy years of exile and 420 years to AD 70, and Rashi identified the anointed prince with Cyrus and the anointed one cut off with Agrippa. Critical scholars, following Porphyry in antiquity and John Collins in modern times, read the weeks against the second century BC: the anointed one cut off is the high priest Onias III, murdered around 171 BC, and the prince who is to come is Antiochus IV, whose desecration of the temple in 167 BC falls in the middle of the last week. They grant that the numbers do not add up exactly, and treat them as schematic.

The traditional Christian reading, held by many church fathers, by Calvin and by interpreters such as E. J. Young, counts sixty-nine weeks from a Persian decree to rebuild Jerusalem to the time of Jesus. The anointed one cut off is Christ crucified, and the people who destroy the city are the Romans of AD 70. Its difficulties are the choice of a starting point and the gap between the cross and AD 70. The dispensational reading agrees that the sixty-nine weeks end with the Messiah, but places a gap before the seventieth week, which it holds is still future. A fourth reading takes the periods as sacred measures rather than calendar years, running from the return to the end of history.

Jerome set out the views of the church fathers and refused to choose among them. Faithful readers differ here, and these notes take no side. They calculate no date from these numbers. The chapter's main point stands on every reading: God has set a limit to his people's suffering, and he will finally deal with sin.
passages.asks: Daniel prayed for the end of seventy years and was told of seventy weeks. Ask how you respond when God's answer is longer than you hoped. And ask whether you can hold on to the promise of verse 24 without needing to work out its timetable.
